overview.title: 📖 Overview: Plucking, Shedding, and a Cryptic Instruction
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 25a–25b
overview.hebrewSource: לֹא בָּזֶה הִתִּיר עֲקַבְיָא בֶּן מַהֲלַלְאֵל, אֶלָּא שְׂעַר בַּעַל מוּם שֶׁנָּשַׁר וְהִנִּיחוֹ בַּחַלּוֹן וְאַחַר כָּךְ מֵת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves Rav Huna's Festival dilemma from 24b by testing and refining exactly what Rav holds about unintentional acts, using a barrel-stopper case and the concept of an inevitable result (פְּסִיק רֵישֵׁיהּ). It then tests whether plucking ever counts as true shearing through Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's surprising leniency about trimming a red heifer's black hair-tips, before refining the original mishna's rules for plucking a firstborn's neck-hair — by hand only, and permitted from the outset even to examine a blemish. A new mishna raises a fresh question: what about hair that sheds from a blemished firstborn while it is still alive? Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis disagree, but only once Rabbi Yosei clarifies which exact scenario they're arguing about. The daf closes with Rav Sheshet's puzzle over a baraita's terse instruction — 'let it be investigated' — which the Gemara connects to no fewer than four different, already-familiar tannaitic disputes.

slides.title: 🍷 Rav's Festival Ruling Reconsidered
slides.subtitle: Testing whether Rav truly permits unintentional acts on a Festival

steps.content: 1️⃣ Challenge: Rav elsewhere forbids tightly inserting a cloth barrel-stopper on a Festival, since liquid is inevitably squeezed out — suggesting Rav forbids unintentional acts generally

2️⃣ Answer: that case is different — even Rabbi Shimon, who usually permits unintentional acts, concedes when the forbidden result is inevitable (פְּסִיק רֵישֵׁיהּ, 'cut off its head and expect it not to die')
3️⃣ Further challenge: doesn't Rav actually rule like Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids unintentional acts as a rule — not like the lenient Rabbi Shimon?

4️⃣ Resolution: Rav does hold an unintentional act is generally forbidden — but he permits plucking a firstborn's hair because plucking is not a form of shearing at all, and on a Festival it counts as an unusual, non-standard way of uprooting growth, which Torah law doesn't prohibit

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: The permission to pluck hair on a Festival rests on redefining the act itself, not on any general leniency for unintentional consequences.

slides.title: 🐄 Does Plucking Ever Count as Shearing?
slides.subtitle: Testing the claim with a bird's feather and a red heifer's hairs

boxes.title: Plucking a Feather = Shearing
items: A baraita: plucking a bird's wing-feather on Shabbat brings liability for shearing
Reish Lakish confirms: plucking IS the normal method for removing feathers, so it counts as shearing there

boxes.title: Plucking Wool ≠ Shearing
items: Wool is normally removed with scissors, not by plucking — so plucking wool is an unusual method, unlike shearing
This is why Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's plucking technique for a firstborn's neck doesn't violate the Torah's shearing ban

boxes.title: The Red Heifer Test Case
items: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam permits trimming two black hair-tips on a red heifer with scissors — an apparent act of true shearing on a consecrated animal
Several explanations are tried and rejected (no wool status; only Temple-maintenance sanctity) before the Gemara settles on: it is simply an uncommon case the Sages' fence never covered

callout.label: Open question:
callout.text: Does Rav's position match Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's reasoning exactly, or do they merely reach the same practical result by different routes?

slides.title: ✂️ Hand or Tool? Ab Initio or After the Fact?
slides.subtitle: Refining exactly how and when a firstborn's hair may be plucked

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: The mishna's permission to clear hair applies only when done by hand — using an actual tool looks too much like deliberate shearing, and is forbidden.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But the mishna explicitly says he clears space 'with a cleaver' (בְּקוֹפִיץ)!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Reread it: he clears space with his hands, in preparation to then use a cleaver for the actual slaughter — not that the cleaver itself plucks the hair.

lines.speaker: New Question
lines.text: Is plucking hair to examine a blemish permitted from the outset (ab initio), or only tolerated after the fact?

lines.speaker: R' Yirmeya's Proof
lines.text: A baraita: wool tangled in a firstborn's ear, hiding a blemish — Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam says one may pluck it outright to show a Sage. This proves it's permitted ab initio.

lines.speaker: Rav Mari
lines.text: Confirmed by the mishna's own comparison: 'and likewise' equates examining a blemish with the original, ab initio permission to pluck for slaughter.

callout.label: Settled:
callout.text: Plucking (never cutting with a tool) is permitted from the very outset, both for slaughter and for blemish examination.

slides.title: 🐑 New Mishna: Hair Shed From a Blemished Firstborn
slides.subtitle: Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis disagree — but about exactly which scenario?
rows: Hair shed while alive, animal later slaughtered
Everyone agrees: the shed hair may be used (per Rabbi Yosei's correction of the dispute)
Hair shed while alive, animal later died naturally (not slaughtered)
Akavya ben Mahalalel: permitted; the Rabbis: forbidden — this is the true point of dispute
Dangling wool that visibly looks part of the fleece
Permitted once the animal is later shorn after death
Dangling wool that does not visibly look part of the fleece

callout.label: Rabbi Yosei's correction:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda first reported the dispute as applying to a slaughtered animal — Rabbi Yosei corrects him: everyone permits that case; the real disagreement is about an animal that simply died.

slides.title: 🔍 Rav Sheshet's 'Let It Be Investigated' Puzzle
slides.subtitle: A baraita's two cryptic words (יְבַקֵּר) get four different explanations

nodes.content: ❓ A blemished firstborn mixes into a flock and is never found. Rabbi Yosei: 'יְבַקֵּר' — let it be investigated. Investigated for what?

columns.label: Reading 1
columns.content: About sheared wool already mixed with ordinary wool — mirrors the Rabbi Yehuda/Rabbi Yosei dispute on a slaughtered firstborn's wool

columns.label: Reading 2
columns.content: Whether an expert had certified the blemish before the wool was shed (Rava's refinement)

columns.label: Reading 3
columns.content: About the animals themselves, when a search failed to find the blemished one — mirrors Rabbi Meir vs. the Rabbis on an unresolved impurity search

columns.label: Reading 4
columns.content: About animals where the blemished one was found — mirrors Rebbi vs. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on a once-lost, now-found grave

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: The Gemara repeatedly explains a difficult local dispute by mapping it onto a structurally identical dispute already known from elsewhere in the Mishna.

summary.principle: Whether an act like plucking counts as forbidden shearing, and whether shed hair or an unfound blemished animal may be treated leniently, all turn on precise definitions of intention, method, and timing rather than blanket rules.

flowSteps.content: 🍷 Rav permits plucking on a Festival because plucking wool is not shearing, not because unintentional acts are generally allowed
🐄 The red heifer's black hair-tips may be trimmed only because that case is uncommon, not because plucking is universally harmless
✂️ Hand-plucking, not tool-cutting, is permitted from the outset — for slaughter and for blemish examination alike

columns.content: 🐑 Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis truly disagree only about hair shed before a natural death, not before slaughter
🔍 'Let it be investigated' recruits four separate, already-familiar disputes to explain one baraita

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Precise definitions of method, timing, and intention — not broad assumptions — determine what counts as forbidden shearing or usable hair

quiz.q: Why does even Rabbi Shimon, who generally permits unintentional acts, agree that tightening a cloth barrel-stopper is forbidden on a Festival?
o: Because Rabbi Shimon never permits any unintentional acts
Because the squeezing out of liquid is an inevitable result of the action (פְּסִיק רֵישֵׁיהּ)
Because barrel-stoppers are always forbidden objects
Because this case involves a firstborn animal
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon concedes an unintentional act is forbidden when the prohibited result is unavoidable and certain to occur — the 'cut off its head and expect it not to die' principle — which applies to squeezing liquid from a tightened stopper.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's final resolution, why does Rav permit plucking a firstborn's hair on a Festival?
o: Because Rav generally permits all unintentional acts
Because plucking wool is not considered a form of shearing at all, making it an unusual (and therefore permitted) form of uprooting growth
Because firstborns are never subject to Festival restrictions
Because Rav retracted his position on unintentional acts entirely
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes that Rav holds unintentional acts are generally forbidden, but permits this specific case because plucking wool by hand is not the normal method of shearing, so it doesn't fall under the Torah's shearing prohibition or its Festival-labor restrictions in the usual way.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara ultimately explain Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's leniency about trimming a red heifer's black hair-tips?
o: Because red heifers have no sanctity whatsoever
Because it is an uncommon case that the rabbinic decree against shearing consecrated animals was never applied to
Because trimming hair-tips is always permitted on any animal
Because the red heifer was already blemished
quiz.e: After testing and rejecting other explanations (lack of wool status, mere Temple-maintenance sanctity), the Gemara settles on the idea that the red heifer is simply so uncommon a case that the Sages' rabbinic fence against shearing consecrated animals was never extended to cover it.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei's clarification, in which scenario do Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis actually disagree about hair shed from a blemished firstborn?
o: When the hair was shed and the animal was later slaughtered
When the hair was shed and the animal later died naturally, without being slaughtered
When the hair was never shed at all
They do not disagree in any scenario
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei corrects the initial framing: everyone agrees shed hair may be used if the animal was subsequently slaughtered. The genuine dispute between Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Rabbis concerns hair shed before the animal died a natural death.

quiz.q: What are two of the different explanations the Gemara offers for Rabbi Yosei's instruction 'let it be investigated' (יְבַקֵּר) regarding a blemished animal lost within a flock?
o: Whether the animal was male or female, and whether it was young or old
Whether an expert certified the blemish before the wool was shed, and whether the search for the animal itself succeeded or failed
Whether the flock belonged to a priest, and whether it was Shabbat
The Gemara offers only one explanation, with no alternatives
quiz.e: Among the readings offered, Rava explains it as asking whether an expert had certified the blemish before the wool was shed, while another version (via Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba/Rabbi Yoḥanan) explains it as asking whether a search for the blemished animal itself succeeded or failed to find it.
